component.name: Apache Kafka
component.description: Distributed event streaming platform: brokers and KRaft controllers exchange records, replication state, and metadata; clients produce and consume over configurable listeners; the Admin API and JMX form a separate control plane. Security (authentication, authorization, transport encryption) is off by default and must be explicitly configured for production.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it. Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams have their own security model pages.

blueprints.name: Kafka cluster deployment
blueprints.description: Brokers expose one or more listeners with independent security configuration (PLAINTEXT, SSL, SASL_PLAINTEXT, SASL_SSL); dedicated inter-broker and controller listeners carry replication and KRaft traffic and should be firewalled off from clients; JMX is an operators-only interface; log segments are written as plain bytes on trusted disks.

assets.name: Kafka brokers
assets.description: Serve producer/consumer traffic and the Admin API over configured listeners; authorization is performed by the configured authorizer (StandardAuthorizer for KRaft clusters) over (principal, host, operation, resource pattern, permission) ACLs.

assets.name: KRaft controllers
assets.description: Exchange metadata with brokers over the controller listeners; the controller listener must never be exposed to client networks.

assets.name: Client-facing listeners
assets.description: Listener protocols selected by listener.security.protocol.map; clients connect to whatever the broker advertises (advertised.listeners) after the initial metadata fetch.

assets.name: JMX interface
assets.description: Operational metrics on brokers, clients, Connect, and Streams; an administrators-only interface, unauthenticated by default.

assets.name: On-disk log segments and metadata
assets.description: Log segments, index files, snapshots, and controller metadata written as plain bytes; at-rest confidentiality is the responsibility of the filesystem, block device, or message-level encryption.

zones.name: Kafka clients
zones.description: Producers, consumers, Admin API clients, Connect workers, and Streams applications connecting over client-facing listeners.

zones.name: Broker and controller fleet
zones.description: Brokers and KRaft controllers; any host that can authenticate on the inter-broker or controller listeners is effectively part of the cluster's trust boundary.

zones.name: Operators
zones.description: Anyone with shell access to a broker, controller, or the underlying disks can read every topic, forge any principal, and rewrite ACLs; the model assumes a trusted operator.

assumptions.description: Kafka trusts its JVM and classpath: JARs on a process's classpath run with that process's full privileges, and the model assumes no hostile JARs are present.
Brokers and KRaft controllers form a trusted fleet; inter-broker and controller listeners are kept on dedicated internal listeners firewalled off from clients.
The data plane, the Admin API, and JMX have distinct authentication and authorization stories that must be configured independently; securing one does not secure the others.

threats.name: Unauthenticated, unencrypted access to a default cluster
threats.description: Security is off by default: a freshly installed cluster accepts unauthenticated PLAINTEXT connections on every listener and applies no authorization, which is appropriate only for closed test environments. An open PLAINTEXT listener with no authorizer is a deployment choice, not a defect; production deployments must explicitly configure authentication, authorization, and transport encryption before exposure to any untrusted network.

threats.name: Authentication configured without an authorizer
threats.description: If no authorizer is configured, all authenticated principals have full access: configuring authentication without an authorizer provides identity but no authorization. Similarly, allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true reverses the default-deny behaviour for resources with no ACLs and is a transitional aid that should not remain set in steady state, and the super.users list bypasses ACL checks entirely and must be treated like a root password.

threats.name: Interception or modification of unencrypted listener traffic
threats.description: Traffic on PLAINTEXT or SASL_PLAINTEXT listeners is unencrypted; the SASL PLAIN mechanism sends username/password in cleartext over the SASL channel and is acceptable only inside a SASL_SSL listener. The security model protects messages in transit when TLS is configured per listener.

threats.name: Controller or inter-broker listener reachable from client networks
threats.description: Brokers and controllers exchange replication state and metadata over the inter-broker and controller listeners; any host that can authenticate on those listeners is effectively part of the cluster's trust boundary, and a compromise of a client-facing listener must not be able to impersonate a broker. Operators must never expose the controller listener to client networks.

threats.name: JMX exposed to non-operators
threats.description: JMX is an administrators/operators-only interface and must never be exposed to actual users; it is unauthenticated by default and should be disabled, bound to localhost with an exporter alongside, or configured with authentication and TLS.

threats.name: Cleartext secrets in configuration files
threats.description: Broker, client, and Connect properties files contain keystore passwords, SASL credentials, and similar secrets; embedding them in version-controlled configuration exposes them. For file-based config providers, an unbounded path also lets a malicious or mistaken configuration coerce the provider into reading arbitrary files on the host.

threats.name: Disclosure of data at rest
threats.description: Kafka does not encrypt log segments, indexes, snapshots, or controller metadata on disk; at-rest confidentiality is disclaimed and is the responsibility of filesystem/block-device encryption, message-level encryption by producers (the only option protecting records from broker operators), or tiered storage with its own encryption.

threats.name: Actions by a trusted operator or broker fleet member
threats.description: Anyone with shell access to a broker, controller, or the underlying disks can read every topic, forge any principal, and rewrite ACLs; the security model does not defend brokers from their own administrators, and a trusted principal performing an authorized operation (including super.users entries) is expected behaviour.

threats.name: Code execution via pluggable interfaces and classpath JARs
threats.description: Every Kafka component exposes pluggable interfaces (authorizers, (de)serializers, connectors, transforms, config providers) loaded by class name that run with the host process's privileges; configuring one is equivalent to running its code, and placing code on the classpath is equivalent to trusting it. The model assumes no hostile JARs; only install plugins you fully trust.

threats.name: Findings in development and test tooling
threats.description: Trogdor is a test framework that injects faults and runs arbitrary user-supplied commands by design and is intended only for development environments; command execution through Trogdor is not a security issue. The tests/ system-test harness and release/ scripts are developer tooling, not components of a running cluster. Out of scope for the security model.

threats.name: Accumulated CVEs in already-released Docker images
threats.description: Published Docker images are free of known CVEs on release day, but the project does not rebuild already-released images, so base layers and bundled dependencies accumulate CVEs not specific to Kafka over time; those are out of scope, and operators are expected to rebuild or patch images for long-running deployments. Only currently supported releases and trunk are in scope for security reports.

trustBoundaries.name: Client listener trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Clients cross into the cluster over listeners whose per-listener protocol determines authentication (none, mTLS, SASL) and encryption (none, TLS); authorization by the configured authorizer arbitrates what an authenticated principal may do. Delegation tokens let authenticated clients fan out short-lived credentials to distributed frameworks.

trustBoundaries.name: Operator and JMX trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The control plane (Admin API, JMX, host shell access) has different exposure than the data plane; JMX must be reserved for operators, and operators themselves are trusted.

controls.name: Configure listener authentication (mTLS and/or SASL)
controls.description: Use TLS client authentication (ssl.client.auth=required, principal derived via ssl.principal.mapping.rules) and/or SASL per listener (GSSAPI/Kerberos, SCRAM-SHA-256/512, OAUTHBEARER with a production JWKS validator, PLAIN only inside SASL_SSL). mTLS is recommended for broker-to-broker and controller-to-broker traffic.

controls.name: Configure an authorizer with least-privilege ACLs
controls.description: Set authorizer.class.name (StandardAuthorizer for KRaft); with an authorizer configured, unmatched access is denied. Keep super.users minimal (it bypasses ACL checks; treat it like a root password) and do not leave allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true in steady state. ACL management APIs are themselves gated by Cluster-resource ACLs.

controls.name: TLS encryption in transit
controls.description: Configure ssl.* per listener; disable TLS below 1.2 and prefer 1.3; set ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm=https on clients (default since 2.0); rotate keystores via dynamic broker configuration to avoid restarts. Connect, MirrorMaker 2, and Streams consume the same ssl.*/sasl.* client configs, so securing the broker is necessary but not sufficient.

controls.name: Separate and firewall internal listeners
controls.description: Keep inter.broker.listener.name and controller.listener.names on a dedicated internal listener (SASL_SSL or SSL) firewalled off from clients; bind external listeners only to interfaces reachable by intended clients; treat advertised.listeners as part of the security configuration; never expose the controller listener to client networks.

controls.name: Distinct keystores for internal and client-facing listeners
controls.description: Use distinct keystores for the inter-broker listener and any client-facing listener so a leaked client-facing key cannot impersonate a broker.

controls.name: Delegation tokens for distributed frameworks
controls.description: Authenticated clients can request short-lived delegation tokens (used as SCRAM credentials) so distributed frameworks fan out to many tasks without distributing the original credential; tokens inherit the requester's principal and ACLs, expire on a fixed schedule, and can be invalidated by the owner.

controls.name: Disable, localhost-bind, or authenticate JMX
controls.description: Either disable JMX, bind it to localhost with an exporter alongside, or configure com.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=true and TLS; never expose it to actual users.

controls.name: Indirect secrets via ConfigProvider with allowed.paths
controls.description: Use ConfigProvider implementations (FileConfigProvider, DirectoryConfigProvider, or custom) instead of embedding cleartext secrets in version-controlled configuration, and set allowed.paths to the specific secret directories so a malicious or mistaken configuration cannot read arbitrary host files.

controls.name: Encrypt sensitive dynamic configs at rest
controls.description: Sensitive dynamic broker configurations are encrypted at rest in the metadata log using password.encoder.secret; rotating that secret requires password.encoder.old.secret and a rolling restart.

controls.name: Ship authorizer and request logs off-broker
controls.description: Authorizer decisions go to the kafka.authorizer.logger log4j logger (INFO records every denied request, DEBUG every allowed one); in regulated environments ship this log to durable, append-only storage off-broker, as there is no built-in tamper-evident audit trail. The kafka.request.logger gives finer per-call detail for forensics but is verbose and off by default.

controls.name: At-rest confidentiality options
controls.description: In increasing order of cost: filesystem or block-device encryption (transparent, protects against disk theft but not broker login); message-level encryption by producers with keys in an external KMS (the only option protecting records from broker operators, but precluding broker-side features that read payloads); or tiered storage with a remote store performing its own encryption.
